result:
JSONL. At ~100 lines a week, the data is small enough that SQLite's advantages never activate, and the costs of a binary format are immediate.

Why:

- Humans read the records. JSONL is readable with `less`, `grep`, `tail -f`, and diff tools. SQLite needs a client for every look.
- Append-only writes on a single thread are the one case JSONL handles safely without coordination. A single `write()` of a line under the pipe-atomicity size lands whole, and there is no concurrent writer to interleave with.
- Version control and review work on text. A run record file can be committed, diffed in a PR, and inspected in a code review. A SQLite file is an opaque blob to every one of those tools.
- Schema changes are free. Add a field and old lines still parse. SQLite needs a migration for the same change, which is real work for a harness this size.
- Recovery from corruption is manual and local: delete or fix the bad line. A damaged SQLite page can take the file with it.

What you give up: no indexed queries, no aggregates without a scan, no constraints. At 5,000 lines a year a full scan with `jq` finishes instantly, so this costs nothing until the volume grows by two or three orders of magnitude or something starts writing concurrently. Both are visible signals, and the migration path is a script that reads the JSONL and inserts rows.
